name: Hungarian Parliament Building
label: Parliament
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Batthyány tér' (4 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Batthyány tér' (node/5217774798): point.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/3199085: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Parliament Building' (295 m across).
notes: The riverside neo-Gothic landmark of Budapest.

text.description:
The Hungarian Parliament is the building most people picture when they think of Budapest: a long, pale neo-Gothic riverfront topped by a central dome. Imre Steindl designed it, and it opened in 1902. It is about 268 m long and 96 m high, and it is still the largest building in Hungary. The height is a nod to the country's 1896 millennium celebrations. The facade is almost perfectly symmetrical, and it carries 242 sculptures inside and out, many of them statues of rulers and military figures. That symmetry is the reason it photographs so well.

The best head-on view is from the Buda side of the Danube, on the embankment beside Batthyány tér. From here you look straight at the river facade, and after dark the lit building can reflect in the water.

If you have time for a second angle, try the Halászbástya (Fisherman's Bastion), where the Parliament appears through white arches and turrets. Another option is Margit híd (Margaret Bridge), which gives a diagonal view with city lights in the foreground. The lower terraces of the Bastion are the safer free choice, because the upper terraces and towers may charge admission. Keep your phone steady by tucking your elbows in against your body, and wait for a gap in the boat traffic if you want a calm reflection.
text.geographic_location: The Parliament stands on Kossuth Square on the Pest bank of the Danube, in central Budapest, with its main facade facing the river. The viewpoint is directly opposite, on the Buda embankment beside Batthyány tér.
text.directions_text: For the viewpoint, take Metro line M2 to Batthyány tér on the Buda side, then walk to the riverside embankment beside the square. The Parliament itself is reached from Kossuth Lajos Square station, which is on Metro line M2 and tram line 2. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) and check how much of the facade fits from where you stand. Switch to the telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for a tighter shot of the dome and towers. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you want a lot of embankment and sky around the building.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Batthyány tér (Buda bank, riverside embankment next to the square, facing the Parliament's river facade). A straight-on, nearly symmetrical view of the Parliament's riverfront facade, which can reflect in the Danube after dark.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the dome on the central vertical line so the two halves of the building balance. Keep the phone level so the long roofline does not slope. If you want the reflection, include some water in the lower part of the frame. For a different angle, try Halászbástya for the arched frame, or Margit híd for a diagonal view.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the building to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the lit facade does not burn out against the dark sky. After dark, use night mode and brace your elbows against your body to keep the phone still. Boats on the river can blur the reflection, so take several shots.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Around sunset and just after, when the building's lights come on.

text.access_note: The view from the Buda embankment is from an open public space, but going inside the Parliament requires a guided tour and photography is restricted in parts of the interior, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Dragging the exposure slider down helps stop the lit facade from burning out against the dark sky.

name: Széchenyi Thermal Bath
label: Széchenyi Baths
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Széchenyi Gyógyfürdő' (2 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OSM R19023 (Széchenyi Thermal Bath): kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Yellow neo-Baroque thermal bath complex in City Park.

text.description:
Széchenyi Thermal Bath is the big yellow bath building in Budapest's City Park (Városliget), and its front is a free, front-on composition that suits a symmetrical shot. The front is symmetrical and Neo-Baroque, so a straight-on shot looks balanced, with the park around it and Vajdahunyad Castle opposite across the road. That mix of warm yellow stonework, trees and a castle makes the picture feel complete without much effort.

The address is Állatkerti körút 9-11. Photographing the front from the street side needs no ticket. The best-known view of the bath is the one of the three large outdoor pools, with steam rising from the water and the yellow main building behind. That view is inside the bath, so you need a bath ticket for it.

For the front, stand square to the middle of the building so the left and right halves match. Because the building is wide, the ultra-wide lens (0.5x) helps you fit it all in from the street. Keep your phone upright and level, using the gridlines, so the walls do not lean. If you go inside, keep your shots on the architecture. Photographing other bathers is frowned upon and staff may stop you. Drones are not allowed over the complex.
text.geographic_location: The bath is in Városliget (City Park) in Budapest, at Állatkerti körút 9-11. Vajdahunyad Castle stands opposite, across the road.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so use a map app to navigate to Állatkerti körút 9-11 in Városliget (City Park). The bath is in City Park, with Vajdahunyad Castle across the road. Once there, the phone icon on the map is right at the building's main front, so there is no further walk. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the whole yellow front in from the street. If you can step back, try the default lens (1x) for a more natural look. On phones with a telephoto (2x-5x), use it for details such as the central part of the façade.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Stand at Széchenyi Gyógyfürdő, on the street side of the main front, facing the building with the park and Vajdahunyad Castle across the road.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Line up the centre of the building with the middle of the screen and turn on the gridlines so both sides match and the walls stay upright. Include a little park greenery for context. For a different view, the three outdoor pools with steam and the yellow building behind them are the classic shot, but that needs a bath ticket and is best kept free of other bathers.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the yellow wall to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a touch if the sky is bright, so the yellow does not wash out. Keep the phone level to avoid leaning walls.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning, when the sun lights the front of the building. The bath is not lit up at night, so evening shots will be dark.

text.access_note: Photographing the front from the street side needs no ticket, but the outdoor-pool view is inside the paid bath, so check the official site before you go.

name: Buda Castle
label: Buda Castle
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Széchenyi István tér' (4 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Széchenyi István tér' (way/23226758): middle (234 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/6486918: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Buda Castle' (388 m across).
notes: Historic royal palace complex crowning Castle Hill.

text.description:
Buda Castle is the great palace complex that stretches along the southern tip of Castle Hill, high above the Danube. The first castle was completed in 1265. The Baroque palace you see today was built between 1749 and 1769, badly damaged in the Second World War and rebuilt in a simpler Baroque style. It now houses the Hungarian National Gallery, the Budapest Historical Museum and the National Széchényi Library.

It photographs best from across the river, where the long palace roofline and dome sit on top of the hill and the Chain Bridge fills the foreground. This is the classic postcard view, and the castle is a long, pale shape that reads well even on a small screen.

A practical warning: large river cruise ships can moor along this stretch of embankment and block the view for much of the year, so glance at the dock before you settle on a spot. If the view is blocked, or you want a quieter option, try Margit híd, which lets you fit the castle, the Parliament and the water tower on Margaret Island into one frame.
text.geographic_location: Buda Castle sits on the Buda side of the Danube, at the southern tip of Castle Hill. The Pest-side view is from the embankment just south of Széchenyi István tér, facing the Chain Bridge.
text.directions_text: Make your way to Széchenyi István tér on the Pest bank of the Danube. The castle is about 700 m away in a straight line to the south-west, across the Chain Bridge, and the Castle Hill Funicular runs up from Clark Ádám Square at the Buda end of the bridge. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x), which fits the bridge and the castle together. Use ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you are close to the bridge and want its full length. If the castle looks small, try telephoto (2x or more) for a tighter shot of the hill.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Széchenyi István tér (on the Pest embankment just south of the square, where the whole bridge span lines up with the castle behind it). The full Chain Bridge in the foreground with Buda Castle rising on the hill behind it. The castle rises on the hill to the south-west, across the water, with the whole Chain Bridge lined up in front of it. The aim is to keep the bridge span and the palace in the same frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the bridge along the lower third, with the castle roofline in the upper half. Keep the phone level so the bridge deck does not slope. If the river view is open, include a strip of water for a clean foreground. For a different angle, Margit híd frames the castle, the Parliament and the Margaret Island water tower together.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the castle to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky does not wash out and the lit buildings keep their colour. After dark, use night mode and rest your elbows on the railing or a wall to keep the phone steady.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Sunset or night, when the castle is lit.

text.access_note: The embankment viewpoint is open public space; the castle's museums and buildings may be ticketed or restricted, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: The Chain Bridge can be crossed on foot from the Pest side to the Buda side.
Large river cruise ships can moor on the Pest embankment and block the view for much of the year (from the viewpoint research).
The castle is lit at night (from the viewpoint research).
Margit híd offers a view with the castle, the Parliament and the Margaret Island water tower in one frame (from the viewpoint research).
Resting your elbows on a railing or wall helps steady a phone for night mode.

name: St. Stephen's Basilica
label: St. Stephen's Basilica
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Zrínyi utca' (2 web pages); placed at the stretch of Zrínyi utca nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OSM R20593057 (St. Stephen's Basilica): kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Neoclassical basilica with a panoramic dome.

text.description:
St. Stephen's Basilica is one of the easiest big buildings in Budapest to photograph well, and the best-known angle is from the street rather than the square. From partway down Zrínyi utca you look back toward the basilica entrance, and the facade sits symmetrically between the buildings on either side. The dome rises above it, so the street works as a ready-made frame. Guides often call this the most photographed view of the basilica, and the default lens (1x) on a phone is wide enough to fit the whole facade in.

Once you have that shot, walk on to Szent István tér for a head-on view of the whole facade and bell towers. There is sky above and cafés and passers-by below, which gives a sense of scale. If you have time and energy, the Citadella gives a very different picture: the dome far away among the bridges, Elisabeth Bridge and the Pest rooftops.

The facade is floodlit after dark, but the lighting times can change, so check current hours locally. In December the square holds a Christmas market, which changes the foreground. Climbing the dome gives city views rather than photos of the church itself, so it is not needed for this shot.
text.geographic_location: On Zrínyi utca, about 146 m west of the basilica and its square, Szent István tér.
text.directions_text: No Underground or tram stop is listed for this spot, so walk in from Szent István tér or the surrounding streets. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x), which fits the full facade between the street buildings. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you are close or want more sky. A telephoto (2x-5x) is good for the dome or the towers.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Zrínyi utca (partway down the street, facing back toward the basilica entrance). The facade lined up symmetrically between the buildings on either side, with the dome rising above, so the street itself acts as a frame. From here the facade lines up symmetrically between the buildings on both sides, with the dome above.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the centre of the doorway with the middle vertical line, so the buildings on each side balance. Keep the phone level to avoid leaning verticals. For a second view, try Szent István tér for a head-on shot with the towers and cafés, or the Citadella for a distant dome among the bridges.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the facade to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the sky stays blue and the stonework keeps its detail. After dark, use night mode and brace your elbows against your body or a wall to keep the shot sharp.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: After dark, when the facade is floodlit, is a good time for night mode, but lighting times can change, so check current hours locally. In December, expect the Christmas market in the square.

text.access_note: The street and square are open to walk, but the dome terrace is a paid climb, so check the official site before you go.

name: Fisherman's Bastion
label: Fisherman's Bastion
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Szent István lovasszobra' (2 web pages); placed at our map tiles: 'Szent István' (pois).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/17948384: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Fisherman's Bastion' (174 m across).
notes: Fairytale terraces with views over the Danube and Pest.

text.description: Fisherman's Bastion is a white, fairytale-looking terrace of arches, stairs and pointed towers on Castle Hill, right beside Matthias Church. It photographs well because the pale stone, the repeated Neo-Romanesque arches and the cone-roofed towers give you strong shapes to work with, and the terraces look out over the Danube. The main façade runs parallel to the river and is roughly 140 metres long. Its seven towers stand for the seven chieftains who founded Hungary in 895. The present structure was built between 1895 and 1902 by the architect Frigyes Schulek, on the base of an older stretch of the castle wall. The name probably comes from the guild of fishermen, who were linked to this part of the wall and to the settlement below it. It is part of the Buda Castle District, which has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1987. For a first photo, start at the statue of King Stephen I in the courtyard in front of Matthias Church. It makes a good foreground, with the church rising behind and the Bastion's towers as a backdrop. Then walk along the terraces and look for arches that frame the river view. The upper terrace and towers are ticketed during the day, while the lower terrace is free. Early arrivals usually find the terraces much emptier. Keep an eye on your bag in the busy spots.
text.geographic_location: In the Buda Castle District on Castle Hill, on the Danube side of Matthias Church. It sits just north of the church courtyard where the statue of King Stephen I stands.
text.directions_text: Head for the Buda Castle District on Castle Hill and make for Matthias Church. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the statue with the church and towers behind it. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the arches and stairs, and to the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for tower roofs and distant details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (in the courtyard in front of Matthias Church, beside the Bastion). The equestrian statue of King Stephen I in the foreground with Matthias Church rising behind it, with the Bastion's towers as backdrop.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Put the statue on one third of the frame and let the church tower and the Bastion's pointed roofs fill the space behind. Turn on gridlines to keep the verticals straight. For a second view, go to the Halászbástya terraces and frame Parliament through the white arches across the Danube. Another option is the stairs beside the Bastion, where the sides frame the towers and city views.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the stone of the church or the towers to set focus, then lower the exposure slider a little if the sky is bright so the white stone keeps its detail. Wipe the lens first, as it picks up fingerprints easily.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early, ideally before about 9 a.m., when the terraces are quietest and you can shoot without crowds in the frame.

text.access_note: The lower terrace is free to enter, but the upper terrace and towers are ticketed during the day, so check the official site before you go for current tickets and hours.
claims_not_in_sources: The Bastion's terraces look out over the Danube towards the Pest side, with Parliament visible across the river.
A bright sky can make white stone look overexposed, so lowering the exposure slider helps keep detail.
Placing the subject on a third of the frame with gridlines on is a simple way to compose the statue shot.

name: Great Market Hall
label: Great Market Hall
camera_source: No separate stand-here point: photographed at the spot itself (indoors, from its top, or right in front of it); drawn as the split pin.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/24323859: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Great Market Hall' (220 m across).
notes: Large covered market with a colourful tiled roof.

text.description:
The Great Market Hall is the largest and oldest indoor market in Budapest, and it works as well as a photo stop as it does for shopping. It opened on 15 February 1897 and was designed by Samu Pecz. The neo-Gothic entrance gate and the steel-framed hall are the main sights. The roof is covered in colourful Zsolnay tiles, which look their best from outside in daylight. The building covers about 10,000 square metres, with stalls on three floors.

Inside, the ground floor is packed with produce, meat, pastries, spices and spirits. Paprika, Tokaji wine and sausages are popular with visitors. Upstairs there are eateries and souvenir stalls, and the basement has fishmongers and pickled vegetables. The hall was badly damaged in World War II. It was restored over several years and reopened in 1997.

For photos, the strongest pictures are the long view down the hall under the iron roof, the colour of the stalls, and close-ups of produce. Keep your phone steady and move slowly, because aisles can be busy. Ask before photographing stallholders or their faces. Step outside to Fővám square for a frame of the entrance and the tiled roof.
text.geographic_location: In Budapest's Pest side, at Fővám square, at the end of the pedestrian shopping street Váci utca and right by the Pest end of the Liberty Bridge.
text.directions_text: Walk to the end of Váci utca (the end by Fővám square), or to the Pest end of the Liberty Bridge, and you will find the hall at Fővám square. No nearby station or tram stop is named here, so from elsewhere in the city centre, walk to Fővám square or look up the route to the Great Market Hall (Nagyvásárcsarnok) on a map app. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the whole hall and roof, then use the default lens (1x) for stalls. Try telephoto (2x-5x) for details such as paprika strings and displays.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. For the building from outside, step out to Fővám square.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line up the main aisle so the roof's steel framework runs straight toward the far end. Keep the ultra-wide level to avoid leaning walls. For stall close-ups, fill the frame with one colourful display, such as red paprika or pastries. Outside, include the neo-Gothic gate and the tiled roof above it.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the brightest part of a stall to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the colours stay rich. If the light is dim, hold the phone steady against a pillar or your elbow, or use night mode for a moment. Use portrait mode only after asking a stallholder.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Go in the morning, when the stalls are freshly laid out and there is usually more room in the aisles. For the outside of the roof, pick a bright, dry daytime so the Zsolnay tiles show their colour.

text.access_note: It is a working public market, so check the official site for current opening times and any rules on photography before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: The stand-here point sits at the middle of the hall, so photographs from it are taken inside the building.
The aisles can be busy, especially at peak times.
The Zsolnay tiled roof is best seen from outside in daylight.
Stallholders may not want to be photographed, so it is polite to ask first.
Mornings are usually quieter and the stalls are freshly set out.
Indoor light in the hall can be dim, so night mode may help.

name: Széchenyi Chain Bridge
label: Chain Bridge
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Széchenyi István tér' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Széchenyi István tér' (way/23226758): middle (234 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/197110386: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Széchenyi Chain Bridge' (472 m across).
notes: Iconic suspension bridge with stone lions.

text.description:
The Széchenyi Chain Bridge is a chain bridge spanning the Danube between Buda and Pest, joining Pest on the east bank to Buda on the west. It was designed by the English engineer William Tierney Clark and built under the Scottish engineer Adam Clark. It opened in 1849 as the first permanent bridge across the river in Hungary, and its main span of 202 metres was among the longest in the world at the time. It was blown up in January 1945 and rebuilt, reopening in 1949. After a long renovation it reopened again in August 2023. Stone lions guard each abutment, carved by János Marschalkó and installed in 1852.

It photographs well because the shape is simple and strong: two stone towers, sweeping chains and a flat deck, with Buda Castle rising on the hill behind. From the Pest embankment you can fit the whole span in one frame, which is the classic postcard view. The bridge is closed to private cars, so the deck is calmer than it used to be. If you walk across, the lions and the ironwork make good close-up subjects.

Start on the Pest side and take the full-span view first. Then cross for details, or try the elevated view from Halászbástya, where the Parliament sits in the same frame. Check the river before you go, because moored cruise ships can block the angle from Pest.
text.geographic_location: In central Budapest, spanning the Danube between Széchenyi István tér in Pest, next to the Gresham Palace and the Hungarian Academy of Sciences, and Clark Ádám tér in Buda, below Castle Hill.
text.directions_text: No tram or Underground stop is listed for this spot, so plan to reach it on foot. Head for Széchenyi István tér on the Pest embankment, next to the Gresham Palace. The middle of the bridge is to the west, about 4 minutes on foot from there. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) held in landscape, which should take in the whole span with the castle behind. If a tower or the far end gets cut off, step back or switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x). For a tighter view that makes the castle look closer to the bridge, try the telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone).
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Széchenyi István tér (Pest embankment, just south of the bridgehead). The whole span of the bridge with Buda Castle rising behind it, the classic postcard composition.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the deck up with a horizontal line so the bridge sits level. Keep both towers in the frame and leave the castle on the hill as the backdrop. If you want a different angle, Halászbástya gives an elevated view with the Parliament in the same frame. Clark Ádám tér, on the Buda side, is better for a close-up of the lions and chains.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the bridge to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the lights keep their colour and the sky does not turn white. Once the light fades, use night mode and rest your elbows or the phone on a wall or railing to keep it steady. Wait for the phone to finish the exposure before you move.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Blue hour, about 15 to 20 minutes after sunset, when the bridge lights are on and the sky still has some colour.

text.access_note: The Pest-side square and embankment are open public space and the bridge is closed to private cars; if you plan to visit Halászbástya, check the official site before you go, as the towers there are ticketed.

name: Shoes on the Danube Bank
label: Shoes on the Danube
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Shoes on the Danube Bank' (3 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/260536715: the OpenStreetMap point 'Shoes on the Danube Bank'.
notes: Memorial of iron shoes along the riverbank.

text.description: This is a memorial, and it works best as a quiet, respectful photograph. Sixty pairs of old-fashioned iron shoes sit along the stone edge of the Danube on the Pest side, some neat, some tipped over, as if just left behind. They remember people who were made to take off their shoes and were shot at the water's edge in the winter of 1944-45, so that the river carried them away. The memorial was unveiled on 16 April 2005, created by film director Can Togay with sculptor Gyula Pauer. Cast-iron signs in Hungarian, English and Hebrew explain it, and a long low stone bench stands behind the shoes. The shoes photograph well because they are simple, close to the ground and set against the wide river. A low angle along the row, with the Parliament or the Buda hills softly behind, tells the story without any fuss. Look for the shoe that stands out to you, such as a child's pair, and let the river blur behind it. Please don't step among the shoes, sit on them or pose in front of them. Treat it as you would a grave, and keep group photos and selfies for somewhere else. Wait a moment for people to move away, then take your picture quietly from the side of the walkway.
text.geographic_location: On the Pest bank of the Danube promenade, about 300 metres south of the Hungarian Parliament and near the Hungarian Academy of Sciences. It lies between Roosevelt Square and Kossuth Square.
text.directions_text: Start from the Hungarian Parliament, which is about 300 metres north of the memorial. Walk south along the Danube promenade to reach the shoes. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the whole row with the river behind. Use the default lens (1x) for a calmer, more natural view. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for a single pair of shoes without leaning over them.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Crouch low and shoot along the row toward the Parliament. The frame shows the full line of iron shoes with the river and the Buda hills, or the Parliament dome in a wide frame, behind them. Keep your feet on the walkway and out of the shoes.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Hold the phone low and aim along the row so the shoes lead the eye towards the Parliament. Turn on gridlines and keep the horizon level. For a closer, more personal picture, frame a single pair at the memorial, perhaps a child's shoe, with the river softly out of focus behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the nearest shoe to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky does not wash out and the iron keeps its detail. If your phone allows portrait mode on objects, it can soften the river further behind a single pair.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon or early morning, when the light is low and the shadows along the row are long.

text.access_note: The memorial stands in an open public space on the riverside promenade, with no ticket needed; it is a Holocaust memorial, so please be respectful and check the official site before you go if you need current details.

name: Gresham Palace
label: Gresham Palace
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Széchenyi István tér' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Széchenyi István tér' (way/23226758): middle (234 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/11847: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Gresham Palace' (101 m across).
notes: Art Nouveau palace facing the Chain Bridge.

text.description:
Gresham Palace is an Art Nouveau building in Budapest. It stands on the Pest bank of the Danube, right beside Széchenyi Square and the Pest end of the Széchenyi Chain Bridge. It was built between 1904 and 1906 as the foreign headquarters of the London-based Gresham Life Assurance Company, with offices and homes for senior staff, and it opened in 1907. It was named after Sir Thomas Gresham, the 16th-century English financier. The architects were Zsigmond Quittner and Jozsef Vago. After decades of decline the building was rebuilt and reopened in 2004 as a luxury hotel, which it still is.

It photographs well because the long, decorated front faces an open square, so you can step back and fit a lot of it in. The best easy spot is the small grassy patch in front of the facade. From there you get the whole front straight on, with the hotel entrance area in the frame. If you would like the palace with water and a bridge around it, the Chain Bridge is a good second choice. It frames the facade with the bridge deck and the Danube. For a higher, more distant view, the upper station of the Buda Castle funicular looks down over the Chain Bridge and the palace. Funicular information we have is from 2022 or earlier and mentions renovation then, so check whether it is running before you plan around it.

The palace is a hotel and its rooms and balconies are private, so take your photos from outside. Keep the phone level and use the gridlines, because a straight-on facade shows up any tilt.
text.geographic_location: In Budapest's city centre on the Pest side of the Danube, facing Széchenyi István tér at the eastern end of the Széchenyi Chain Bridge.
text.directions_text: Head for Széchenyi István tér, the square at the Pest end of the Chain Bridge. The small grassy patch in front of the facade is the suggested viewpoint, with the hotel entrance behind it. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for a straight-on view of the whole front. If the facade will not fit from the grass, switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x). Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details of the upper floors and decoration.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Széchenyi István tér (the grass patch directly in front of the palace's facade). The full front facade of the palace straight on, with the hotel entrance area in the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Centre yourself on the entrance and turn on the gridlines so the vertical lines of the building stay straight. Keep the phone upright and level to avoid leaning walls. For a different view, try the Chain Bridge, where the bridge deck and the Danube frame the facade.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the facade to set focus, then lower the exposure slider slightly if the sky is bright, so the stonework and decoration keep their detail. For evening shots, use night mode and hold the phone steady against your body or a solid surface.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Choose a time when the sky is fairly clear and the light is soft, as this helps the stonework and decoration show up well. Early morning is usually the easiest time to avoid people on the square.

text.access_note: The square and the grass patch in front are outdoors, but the palace is a hotel with private rooms and balconies, so check the official site before you go if you want to see inside.
claims_not_in_sources: The square is usually quieter early in the morning.
The grass patch in front of the palace is reachable on foot from the square.

name: Hungarian State Opera House
label: State Opera House
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Andrássy út' (4 web pages); placed at the stretch of Andrássy út nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/24000390: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Hungarian State Opera House' (146 m across).
notes: Neo-Renaissance opera house on Andrássy Avenue.

text.description: The Hungarian State Opera House is a neo-Renaissance building with Baroque touches, designed by Miklós Ybl. Building began in 1875 and it opened on 27 September 1884. It photographs well because the front is symmetrical and the decoration follows a musical theme. Statues of the composers Ferenc Erkel and Franz Liszt, by Alajos Stróbl, stand in niches either side of the main entrance. After a long restoration the house reopened on 12 March 2022, so the exterior should look in good shape. The best photo is straight-on from the far pavement of Andrássy út, directly across from the façade. From there you can fit in the whole front: the arcaded loggia, the central entrance and the statues along the roofline. The Opera House is to the north-west of you. Keep your phone level and use the gridlines so the vertical lines of the building stay straight. If you cannot fit it all in at the default lens (1x), step back or switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x), but watch for stretched edges. For a second view, stand further along the tree-lined avenue and zoom in. The trees then lead the eye towards the building. Photographing the outside needs no ticket. Pictures of the interior are a different matter, so check the official site before you go if you want to see inside.
text.geographic_location: In central Budapest, on Andrássy út at number 22.
text.directions_text: Go to Andrássy út 22, the Opera House address. Cross to the far pavement, straight opposite the main entrance. Use the pedestrian crossings and keep clear of the traffic when you step back to frame the photo. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x). Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) if the façade will not fit, and the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the compressed view along the avenue.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Andrássy út (opposite (far) sidewalk, straight across from the façade). The full neo-Renaissance front of the Opera House framed straight-on, with its symmetry, arcaded loggia and roofline statues. The Opera House is to the north-west of you, so face it square-on for a symmetrical shot.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and centre the main entrance on the middle line. Hold the phone level so the building does not lean. Include the loggia and the roofline statues, and leave a little space above the roof. For a different view, move along the avenue and zoom in so the trees and street lead towards the building.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the façade to focus, then lower the exposure slider a little at dusk so the lit stonework does not wash out. In the evening, use night mode and brace your elbows against your body to keep the shot steady.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Dusk or evening, when the façade is lit. Early morning is another option for softer light.

text.access_note: The exterior can be photographed freely from the street; for any visit inside, check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: The Opera House is in Budapest's 6th district (Terézváros).
The façade is lit in the evening and looks good at dusk.
Early morning light from the east may suit the façade.
The far pavement of Andrássy út has room to step back and frame the whole front.
The stand-here point is about a minute on foot from the entrance (from the 85 m distance given).
Ultra-wide shots can stretch objects near the edges of the frame.

name: Heroes' Square
label: Heroes' Square
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Hősök tere' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Hősök tere' (way/189829264): middle (48 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/6411893: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Heroes' Square' (240 m across).
notes: Millennium Monument with statues of Hungarian leaders.

text.description: Heroes' Square is one of Budapest's big set-piece squares, and it works well on a phone because everything is laid out in one wide, symmetrical frame. A curved pair of colonnades holds bronze statues of Hungarian rulers and national leaders. In the middle a tall column carries the Archangel Gabriel, who holds the Holy Crown of Hungary. Building began in 1896 for the thousandth anniversary of the Hungarian conquest of the Carpathian Basin and was mostly finished by 1900. The angel stands 4.8 m high on a column of about 36 m, and the monument was inaugurated in 1905. The square has been officially called Heroes' Square since 1932. It sits at the outbound end of Andrássy Avenue, next to City Park, with the Museum of Fine Arts and the Hall of Art on either side. The best view of the full run of the colonnades and the central column comes from the back of the square near the Millennium Monument. Stand back far enough to fit the whole thing in, and keep the column in the middle so the two colonnades balance. A second option is to shoot from Andrássy Avenue, using the zoom to layer trees and traffic in front of the monument. Traffic circles the square, so use the marked crossings and keep an eye on cars if you step to the edges. Tour groups tend to arrive later in the day, so earlier visits are quieter.
text.geographic_location: Heroes' Square is in Budapest at the outbound end of Andrássy Avenue, beside City Park. The Museum of Fine Arts and the Hall of Art face each other across it.
text.directions_text: No Underground or tram stop is listed for this spot, so head for Andrássy Avenue and follow it out to its outbound end, where it meets the square. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the whole colonnade and column in one frame. Then try the default lens (1x) for a calmer, more symmetrical view. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details such as the statues or the angel on top of the column.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Hősök tere (back of the square, near the Millennium Monument). The full run of the colonnades and the central column with Archangel Gabriel, framed as a wide view of the whole monument. The middle of the square lies to the south-west of this point.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the column up with the centre of the frame so the two colonnades sit evenly on each side. Hold the phone level, because tilting it makes the columns lean. For an alternative, walk to Andrássy Avenue and use the telephoto to frame the square and its statues from a distance, with trees and traffic layered in front.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the monument to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky looks washed out. At blue hour, switch on night mode and brace your elbows against your body so the floodlit statues stay sharp.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Sunrise gives the emptiest square. Blue hour suits the floodlit statues. Tour groups arrive later in the day.

text.access_note: Heroes' Square is an open public square, open around the clock and free to enter; check the official site before you go if you plan to visit the museums beside it.

name: Gellért Thermal Bath
label: Gellért Baths
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Szent Gellért tér' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Szent Gellért tér – Műegyetem' (node/5217774785): point.
pin_note: Position from OSM R3363212 (Rác Thermal Bath): kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Art Nouveau thermal bath beside Liberty Bridge.

text.description:
The Gellért Thermal Bath is an Art Nouveau bath building on the Buda bank of the Danube, with Gellért Hill rising behind it and the Liberty Bridge beside it. It photographs well because the facade is formal and detailed, and the bridge pylons give you a strong landmark to include in the frame.

The best everyday view is from Szent Gellért tér, the square directly opposite the bath entrance. A Hungarian heritage guide describes it as one of the finest squares in Buda. Standing there, you can take a straight-on shot of the front of the building, with the Liberty Bridge pylons showing beside it.

The bath is currently closed for a major renovation, expected to last until about 2028. That means only the outside can be photographed, and the famous indoor pool pictures are not possible. Check the current status before you travel.

From the square, start with the whole building in one frame, then move in for details such as the entrance and the stonework. If you want a different angle, the Liberty Bridge shows the building in the foreground with Gellért Hill behind it and the Danube in front. Gellért Hill itself gives a wide view that takes in the bath, the river, the bridge and the city.

Early morning or late afternoon is the best time, when a tourism guide says the light on the facade is soft and warm.
text.geographic_location: The bath is on the Buda bank of the Danube, with Gellért Hill behind it and the Liberty Bridge beside it. The viewpoint is Szent Gellért tér, the square opposite the entrance.
text.directions_text: Head to Szent Gellért tér, opposite the bath entrance. When you reach the square, stand facing the bath entrance. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the whole facade and the bridge pylon into one frame. Use the default lens (1x) for a more natural look, and the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details of the entrance and stonework.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Szent Gellért tér (in front of the bath entrance). The bath's facade from the square, with the Liberty Bridge pylons visible beside it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on the gridlines and line the front of the building up with them so the verticals stay straight. Keep your phone level; tilting it upwards makes the building lean. For a different view, the Liberty Bridge shows the bath in the foreground with Gellért Hill behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the facade to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright, so the stonework keeps its detail.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon, when the light on the facade is soft and warm.

text.access_note: Viewing from the square is free, but the bath itself is closed for renovation until about 2028, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Tilting a phone upwards makes tall buildings appear to lean (general photographic point).
Lowering the exposure slider helps keep detail when the sky is bright (general photographic point).

name: Dohány Street Synagogue
label: Great Synagogue
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Dohány utca' (2 web pages); placed at the stretch of Dohány utca nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/223530620: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Dohány Street Synagogue' (108 m across).
notes: Largest synagogue in Europe, in Moorish Revival style.

text.description:
The Dohány Street Synagogue is the largest synagogue in Europe, and from across the street it is easy to see why people stop for a photo. The front is built in a Moorish style, with alternating yellow and red brickwork, a rose window above the main entrance and two octagonal towers topped with onion domes at about 43 metres. Ludwig Förster, the Viennese architect, designed it, and it was built between 1854 and 1859. It was consecrated in September 1859 and originally seated nearly 3,000 people. The whole building is about 75 metres long and 27 metres wide.

For a phone, the striped front and the twin towers make a strong, symmetrical subject. The façade looks onto a small, irregularly shaped square rather than a broad plaza, so the trick is to find enough distance to fit the towers in. Crossing to the opposite side of Dohány utca gives you that, and the towers can then be seen in full from base to dome. The complex also includes a museum, the Heroes' Temple, a memorial and a graveyard. The courtyard contains the graves of people who died in the ghetto in the winter of 1944-45, so treat it as a place of remembrance and not as a backdrop for posed portraits. If you do go into the Raoul Wallenberg Memorial Park, the silver weeping-willow sculpture is a quieter second picture.
text.geographic_location: On Dohány utca in Erzsébetváros, Budapest's 7th district, in Pest. Dohány Street was the border of the Budapest Ghetto during the Holocaust. The synagogue stands beside the Hungarian Jewish Museum and the memorial courtyard.
text.directions_text: No Underground or tram stop was given for this spot, so head for Erzsébetváros (the 7th district) in central Pest, by taxi or hired scooter if you are coming from further away, and ask for Dohány utca. Once you are on Dohány utca the building is hard to miss. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you are standing close, so both towers and the domes fit. If there is room to step back, the default lens (1x) gives a more natural look with less stretching at the edges.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Dohány utca (opposite (west) side of Dohány Street, across from the main facade). The full height of the twin towers and the striped facade, framed from across the street.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line the central axis of the façade up with the middle grid line, so the two towers sit evenly. Hold the phone level and tilt it as little as you can, to stop the towers leaning inwards. If you want a different angle, the Raoul Wallenberg Memorial Park offers the silver willow sculpture with the synagogue's buildings around it.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brightest part of the brickwork to set focus, then lower the exposure slider a little so the sky does not wash out and the red and yellow stripes keep their colour.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon, when the light is softer and there are fewer people in the street.

text.access_note: The street view is from public pavement, but entry to the synagogue, courtyard and memorial park may need a ticket and photography can be restricted during services, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Using the ultra-wide lens (0.5x) helps fit both towers into the frame when standing close.
Tilting the phone upwards makes tall buildings appear to lean inwards.
Lowering the exposure slider helps keep colour in bright brickwork against the sky.
The pavement opposite the synagogue on Dohány utca is public and free to stand on.

name: Vajdahunyad Castle
label: Vajdahunyad Castle
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Városliget' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Városliget' (relation/3233021): edge nearest the subject (2377 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/275019091: the OpenStreetMap point 'Vajdahunyad Castle'.
notes: Castle in City Park mixing several Hungarian architectural styles.

text.description:
Vajdahunyad Castle looks like a whole history of Hungarian architecture packed into one park. The main facade copies the Hunyadi Castle in Vajdahunyad (now Hunedoara, Romania), and the rest of the complex mixes Romanesque, Gothic, Renaissance and Baroque parts. It was designed by Ignác Alpár and first built in 1896 for the Millennial Exhibition, originally from wood and cardboard. It was rebuilt in brick and stone between 1904 and 1908, so what you see today is the lasting version.

It photographs well because the towers and rooflines are so varied, and because the lake in front of them gives you a second picture in the water. The best-known angle is from the lakeside path in Városliget, near the ice rink. From there you can fit the full height of the facade into the frame, with the towers reflected on calm water. If the lakeside is busy or the water is rippled, go into the courtyard instead. There you can frame stone arches, carved details and the statue of Anonymus, the unknown chronicler at the court of King Béla III. A second option is the footbridge, which gives a symmetrical view with the castle and bridge in the water. In winter the ice rink and event setups can block the best angles from the bridge.

The castle also houses the Museum of Hungarian Agriculture, so the building is a working museum as well as a photo stop. Allow time to walk around it, as every side looks different.
text.geographic_location: Vajdahunyad Castle stands in Városliget, the City Park of Budapest. The lake lies in front of it, and the lakeside path with the ice rink is the usual place for photographs.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so head for Városliget (City Park). From there the castle is about 344 m to the north-east. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the full facade and its reflection. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want to include more of the water and sky. Use telephoto (2x-3x, depending on your phone) for towers and carved details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Városliget (lakeside path near the ice rink, across the water from the castle facade). The castle towers reflected in the lake, with the full height of the facade visible from the water's edge.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the waterline roughly across the middle of the frame, so the towers and their reflection take equal space. Crouch slightly to bring the water closer. For a quieter alternative, shoot the arches and the Anonymus statue in the courtyard, or try the symmetrical view along the footbridge.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the towers to set focus, then lower the exposure slider a little so the sky does not wash out. Hold the phone still, as the reflection looks softer if it moves.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Before 9 a.m. on a calm morning, when the lake is still and the paths are nearly empty.

text.access_note: The castle courtyards are described as open around the clock, but the museum has opening hours and may need a separate photo ticket, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Gridlines help keep the towers and the waterline level in the frame.
Lowering the exposure slightly helps keep bright sky detail.
The ultra-wide lens (0.5x) can include more water and sky but may make buildings at the edges look stretched.
Crouching lower makes the reflection fill more of the frame.

name: Gellért Hill
label: Gellért Hill
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Szabadság-szobor' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Szabadság-szobor' (node/1488974596): point.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/963923001: the OpenStreetMap point 'Gellért Hill'.
notes: Hilltop with sweeping views over the Danube and the city.

text.description: Gellért Hill is the steep, parkland-covered hill on the Buda bank of the Danube. It is 235 m high, and the Citadella at the top stands about 140 m above the river. That height is why it photographs so well. From the terrace below the Liberty Statue (Szabadság-szobor) you look across the water to the Chain Bridge, Elisabeth Bridge and the Parliament, with the Pest skyline spread out in front of you. The Citadella was built by the Habsburgs after the 1848-49 uprising, partly so that guns could command both Buda and Pest. The Liberty Statue beside it was put up by the Soviet Red Army to mark its Second World War victory. Since 1987 the hill has been part of the UNESCO World Heritage site 'the Banks of the Danube'. For phone photos, the terrace gives a wide, layered view: river in the middle, bridges as leading lines, and the city behind. Some guides say the lookouts on the way up frame the river better now that trees near the summit have grown, so pause at them as you climb. The Citadella has been through a long renovation, and parts of the hilltop may still be fenced off, so expect some barriers in the background of wide shots.
text.geographic_location: Gellért Hill is on the Buda side of the Danube, in the 1st and 11th districts. Gellért Square, Hotel Gellért and the Gellért Baths sit at its foot, next to Liberty Bridge.
text.directions_text: No Underground, tram or rail stop is listed for this spot, so take the walking path up to the Citadella and the Liberty Statue. The path climbs steadily, so allow time and wear comfortable shoes. Bus 27 also goes up to the Liberty Statue. Check the current state of the hilltop before you set out. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole river view. Switch to telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the Parliament or the Chain Bridge. Use ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you want the statue or the sweep of the terrace in the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (terrace below the statue, on the Citadella side of the summit). The Danube with the Chain Bridge, Elisabeth Bridge and the Parliament across the river, with the Pest skyline in front of you.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the river on the lower third line, keeping the horizon level. Use the bridges as lines leading to the Parliament. For a second angle, try the lookouts on the way up, which some guides say frame the river better now. For a different view, shoot the hill itself from Március 15. tér, where Elisabeth Bridge sits in the middle distance with Gellért Hill behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the Parliament or the bridges to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky keeps its colour. Try panorama for the full river sweep, moving slowly and keeping the phone upright. After sunset, use night mode and brace your elbows on the railing or a wall to keep the shot sharp.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Golden hour before sunset, then blue hour.

text.access_note: The terrace below the Liberty Statue is free to reach on foot, but the Citadella has had long renovation work and some areas may be closed, so check the official site before you go; the Tetőkert 360 roof garden and rondella terrace need a separate exhibition ticket.

name: Margaret Island
label: Margaret Island
camera_source: Commons cluster (5 photos), weak.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/3232203: large area 'Margaret Island' (3297 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.
notes: Green island park in the middle of the Danube.

text.description: Margaret Island is a long, green strip in the middle of the Danube, between Margaret Bridge to the south and Árpád Bridge to the north. It is about 2.5 km long and 500 m wide, and most of it is landscape park. For a phone photographer it works as a scene rather than a single landmark. You get water on both sides, wide lawns and tree-lined paths, plus a few clear subjects to point at: the octagonal Art Nouveau Water Tower from 1911, the Centennial Memorial of 1973 and the Music Fountain near Margaret Bridge. The ruins of medieval churches and convents are a reminder that the island was a religious centre in the Middle Ages. It takes its name from Saint Margaret, daughter of King Béla IV, who lived in the Dominican convent here. It became a public garden in 1908. Today it is a popular place for a stroll or a run, and cars are largely kept out, so the paths feel calm. Start with a wide shot to show the island in its river setting. Then move closer for details such as the Water Tower, the fountain or a ruined wall framed by trees. Keep the horizon level with the gridlines on, and take a few frames as you walk, because the view changes with every bend in the path.
text.geographic_location: Margaret Island sits in the Danube in central Budapest, between Margaret Bridge and Árpád Bridge, and is run directly by the city rather than by a district.
text.directions_text: No Underground or tram stop is listed for this spot, so start from central Budapest and head for Margaret Bridge, the island's southern gateway. Cars are mostly kept off the island; only a single bus line and taxis may enter, so plan to walk once you arrive. The phone icon on the map is about 500 m north-east of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the whole island and river. Switch to the default lens (1x) for paths and lawns, and to telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details such as the Water Tower.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 500 m north-east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south-west. Once on the island, stand on a path with the trees and water on either side of you for a framed view.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Use the gridlines and place the horizon on the upper or lower third line. Look for a foreground, such as a path, a bench or overhanging branches, to give the wide shots depth. For the Water Tower or the Music Fountain, step back and use 2x or more so the building stays straight and does not lean.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the main subject to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky or water is bright. Use Live Photos near the fountain to catch the moving water, and portrait mode for a person against the greenery.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and fewer people on the paths. In summer the Music Fountain has music and light shows, so a visit in the evening may suit it. Check the official site for times.

text.access_note: The island is a public garden, but some venues on it, such as the water park, the Water Tower exhibition and the open-air theatre, may be ticketed or have set hours, so check the official site before you go.

name: Matthias Church
label: Matthias Church
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Halászbástya' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Halászbástya' (relation/17948384): middle (174 m across); moved 5 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/37135081: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Matthias Church' (83 m across).
notes: Gothic church with a colourful tiled roof on Castle Hill.

text.description:
Matthias Church is the colourful centrepiece of Buda's Castle District, standing on Holy Trinity Square right in front of the Fisherman's Bastion. The present building is late Gothic, dating from the second half of the 14th century, and it was heavily restored in the late 19th century. It is best known from outside for its patterned, Zsolnay-tiled roof and its spires. Inside, it has a long royal story: the last two Kings of Hungary, Franz Joseph I and Charles IV, were crowned here. King Matthias rebuilt the southern tower in 1470, and since the 19th century the church has been called Matthias Church after him.

It photographs well because the roof and spires sit right beside the white towers of the Bastion, and the Bastion's arches make a natural frame. The simplest postcard angle is from the lower terrace of the Halászbástya, looking at the church roof from among the Bastion's towers. From there you get the tiles, the spires and the stonework in one picture. You do not need to go inside for these shots. If you want a different view, Szentháromság tér gives a ground-level picture with the church roof in the frame and the Bastion towers rising behind it.

The square is quietest at sunrise. Mid-morning and summer are the busiest times, so expect people in your frame then. Take a few shots with and without a doorway or arch in front, and check the results before you move on.
text.geographic_location: In the heart of Buda's Castle District, on Holy Trinity Square (Szentháromság tér), directly in front of the Fisherman's Bastion.
text.directions_text: No Underground or tram stops are listed for this spot, so start from the Castle District in Buda and head for Holy Trinity Square. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the Bastion's arches together with the roof and spires. Use the default lens (1x) for a cleaner, more natural view. Switch to telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the tiled roof pattern and the spires.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Halászbástya (lower/central terrace, facing the church roof from the Bastion's towers). The church's colourful tiled roof and spires rising beside the white towers of the Bastion, with the Bastion's arches framing the scene. From here the church lies to the south-west.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on the gridlines and place the roofline on the upper line so the tiles fill the top of the frame. Use an arch of the Bastion as a natural frame around the spires. For an alternative, try a ground-level view from Szentháromság tér, with the Bastion towers rising behind the church roof.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the tiled roof to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the bright sky does not wash out the colours. Check your shot by zooming in on the screen to make sure the roof detail is sharp.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Sunrise, when the square is empty and the light is warm. Late afternoon light can also work well on the roof. Avoid mid-morning and summer peaks if you want clear frames.

text.access_note: The lower terrace of the Fisherman's Bastion is free to enter, but the upper level is ticketed and the church is a place of worship that closes to visitors during services, so check the official sites before you go.

name: Váci Street
label: Váci Street
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Vörösmarty tér' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Vörösmarty tér' (relation/3228022): middle (220 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/18737184: large area 'Váci utca' (1098 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.
notes: Famous pedestrian shopping street in central Pest.

text.description: Váci utca is one of the main pedestrian streets of central Budapest, and perhaps the most famous. It is named after the city of Vác and is lined with cafés, restaurants and shops aimed at visitors. It is busy and touristy, but the long, car-free corridor of façades is easy to photograph. The best wide view is from its northern end, where the street opens onto Vörösmarty tér. From the square you can look south down the whole street as it recedes towards Ferenciek tér. The Gerbeaud café and the Vörösmarty statue give the foreground something solid to anchor the picture. Because the square opens up the view, it is the widest composition you will get of the street. Late afternoon suits this view well, as the low sun throws long shadows between the buildings. For a clearer, quieter street, try a weekday morning before 9 AM. In winter a Christmas market on the square can block the view and add crowds. Further along the street, a mural of Saint George slaying a dragon and the Serbian Orthodox church of Saint George make good extra shots. If a stranger invites you into a bar, politely decline, as the street is known for scams of that kind.
text.geographic_location: Váci utca is a pedestrian street in central Budapest. Its northern end opens onto Vörösmarty tér, next to the Gerbeaud café.
text.directions_text: No nearby station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so walk or use your own navigation to Vörösmarty tér in central Budapest. The subject is about 315 m to the south-east, a walk of roughly 5 minutes. Walk down the pedestrian street to see more of it. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the full length of the street and the square in one frame. Then switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural view. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pull the distant end of the street closer.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Vörösmarty tér (northern end of Váci utca, looking south down the street). The full length of the pedestrian street receding south toward Ferenciek tér, with the Gerbeaud café and Vörösmarty statue framing the foreground. From here the whole pedestrian street runs away from you towards Ferenciek tér.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the street's vanishing point near the centre, with the café and statue low in the frame. Keep your phone level so the building lines stay straight. For a different picture, walk a little way down for a street-level view towards the Saint George church in the distance. Kristóf tér also has the Hermes and Fisher Girl fountains for close-up details.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the sunlit part of the street to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the bright patches don't wash out. Wait a moment for people to move through the frame, or take a Live Photo and choose the cleanest moment.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon, when the low sun casts long shadows between the buildings. For fewer people, go on a weekday before 9 AM.

text.access_note: Váci utca is a public pedestrian street, but Vörösmarty tér hosts a Christmas market in winter, so check the official site before you go if you plan to visit then.
claims_not_in_sources: From the stand-here point the walk to the subject is about 5 minutes (315 m x 1.3 / 80 m per minute).

name: Liberty Statue
label: Liberty Statue
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Szabadság-szobor' (2 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/1488974596: the OpenStreetMap point 'Liberty Statue'.
notes: Monumental statue on top of Gellért Hill.

text.description:
The Liberty Statue, also called the Freedom Statue (Szabadság-szobor), stands on the summit of Gellért Hill at the east end of the Citadella. The bronze figure is 14 m tall and holds a palm leaf above its head. It stands on a 26 m pedestal, so it rises well above the hilltop. It was first put up in 1947 and was designed by Zsigmond Kisfaludi Strobl. Its inscription was changed after 1989, and it now remembers those who gave their lives for Hungary's independence, freedom and prosperity.

It photographs well because of where it stands. From the terrace by the statue you look across the Danube to the Pest side, with Parliament and the rest of the skyline behind the bronze. Visitors often treat this as the classic shot, and the railing near the statue is a good place to try for the Parliament view.

Up close the figure is very tall, so step back along the terrace and tilt the phone upwards to fit more of it in. Keep the statue to one side of the frame and let the river and city fill the rest. If you have time, you can also photograph the statue from below. From the Buda approach of Elisabeth Bridge, or from the Liberty Bridge area, it crowns the hilltop above the bridge, which makes a different, wider picture. The summit shot is the most direct one.
text.geographic_location: On the summit of Gellért Hill, at the east end of the Citadella, on the Buda bank of the Danube. It looks across the river towards the Pest side.
text.directions_text: No Underground or tram stop is listed for this spot, so head for the Citadella on the Gellért Hill summit on the Buda side of the river. The statue is at the east end of the Citadella. Once you are on the summit, head for the terrace by the statue that faces the Pest side. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the tall statue and the city in one frame. Then use the default lens (1x) for a cleaner view, and the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out Parliament across the river.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Stand at the Szabadság-szobor, on the statue terrace on the Gellért Hill summit, facing the Pest side. From here the photo shows the bronze statue in the foreground, with the Danube, Parliament and the Pest skyline behind it. The railing near the statue is a good spot for the Parliament view.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on the gridlines and put the statue on one of the vertical lines, leaving the river and skyline on the other side. Keep the horizon level. If you want the statue to look as tall as it is, tilt the phone up from a little way back with the ultra-wide (0.5x). For a different picture, try the statue on its hilltop from the Buda approach of Elisabeth Bridge or from the Liberty Bridge area. In the Liberty Bridge shot, the green ironwork and passing trams make a good foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the sky or the bright part of the city to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky stays blue and the bronze does not go flat. At dusk, night mode helps with the city lights, but rest your elbows on the railing to keep the phone steady.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Golden hour and blue hour, when the city lights come on. One guide suggests arriving 30 to 45 minutes before sunset.

text.access_note: Gellért Hill and the statue are free to visit, but the Citadella area has been under renovation and some parts may have limited access, so check the official site before you go.

name: Liberty Bridge
label: Liberty Bridge
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Fővám tér' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Fővám tér' (node/6376038704): point.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/197315957: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Liberty Bridge' (354 m across).
notes: Green Art Nouveau bridge over the Danube.

text.description: Liberty Bridge is the green steel bridge linking Pest and Buda across the Danube, and it is one of the easiest bridges in Budapest to photograph. It was built between 1894 and 1896 as part of the Millennium celebrations and first named after Emperor Franz Joseph, who inserted the last silver rivet himself. It is only about 334 metres long, so on a phone the whole span fits in one frame. From the Pest end, the ironwork rises toward Gellért Hill and the hill sits behind it. That gives the picture a clear foreground, middle and background. Look for the Art Nouveau details too: large bronze Turul birds, a falcon-like bird from Hungarian legend, sit on top of the four masts, and the country's coat of arms decorates the sides. Trams cross the bridge, which adds colour and a sense of scale. The Pest end, Fővám tér beside the Great Market Hall, is the spot guides recommend for shooting toward Buda. The light is at its warmest there as the sun drops, and the city lights come on behind the span after dark. Start with the full span, then move closer for a detail of the masts or a Turul. If you want a second angle, Szent Gellért tér on the Buda side shows the trams on the bridge with the Pest riverfront behind. Take care near the ironwork and stay on the walkways.
text.geographic_location: Liberty Bridge crosses the Danube at the southern end of Budapest's city centre, joining Fővám tér in Pest (beside the Great Market Hall) with Gellért tér in Buda, at the foot of Gellért Hill.
text.directions_text: Head for Fővám tér, beside the Great Market Hall at the Pest end of the bridge. Check a local map for how to get there from where you are staying. From there the middle of the bridge is to the west, about 3 minutes on foot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to get the whole green span in one frame. Switch to telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for details such as a Turul on a mast or a tram crossing. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you want the market hall and the square in the frame as well.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Fővám tér (Pest bridgehead, beside the Great Market Hall). The full green span of the bridge rising toward Gellért Hill, with the hill behind the ironwork.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line the bridge up along one of them so the span looks level and the masts stay upright. Put the hill behind the ironwork and wait for a yellow tram to cross if you can. For a different view, Szent Gellért tér on the Buda side shows trams on the green bridge with the Danube and the Pest riverfront behind. The terrace by the Gellért Hill Cave Church looks diagonally across the river toward Pest. The Citadella at the top of the hill was reported as under restoration, so stick to the lower viewpoints.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the green steel to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky keeps its colour and the bridge is not washed out. After dark, use night mode and rest your elbows on a wall or railing to keep still. Stay on the walkways and do not climb on the ironwork.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Sunset, arriving about an hour early so you can try angles while the warm light hits the green steel and then shoot as the city lights come on.

text.access_note: The bridge and Fővám tér are public places, but check local signs and the official city information before you go in case of closures or restrictions, and stay on the walkways.
claims_not_in_sources: Trams on the bridge are yellow (from the researched viewpoint notes, a travel-guide source).
A 2x telephoto setting is useful for framing details such as the Turul statues; exact zoom levels depend on the phone.
Fővám tér and the bridge are open public spaces without an entry ticket.
Resting your elbows on a wall or railing helps keep a night-mode photo steady.
